options: 80% attendance – you may miss at most two practical classes
questions.explanation: 80% attendance (able to miss two practical classes); tutorial and case presentations are mandatory. (Introduction)

questions.q: To pass OMT II you need 50% overall AND:
options: An average of 50% in the two practical exams
A pass in the case study only
questions.explanation: Subject requirements: ≥50% overall and an average of 50% in the two practical exams. (Introduction)

questions.q: Travell's definition describes a trigger point as a hyper-irritable spot in skeletal muscle associated with:
options: A hypersensitive palpable nodule in a taut band
questions.explanation: "A hyper-irritable spot in skeletal muscle associated with a hypersensitive palpable nodule in a taut band…" with referred pain, motor dysfunction and autonomic phenomena. (TrP Part 1)

questions.q: The lecture compares trigger-point referral to a leaky water pistol because:
options: Referral can include the area between the trigger point and the distant painful point
The pain is always wet and burning
Pain only appears exactly at the trigger point
questions.explanation: The pistol wets a distant point and often everything in between. (TrP Part 1 / study pack)

questions.q: Who coined the term "myofascial trigger point" in the 1950s?
questions.explanation: Balfour 1816 "nodular tumours", Froriep 1843 "muskelschwiele", Schade 1919 "myogeloses", Kellgren saline maps, Travell & Rinzler 1950s "myofascial trigger point". (TrP Part 1)

questions.q: Which type of trigger point is the most painful and usually located at the neuromuscular (innervation) point?
questions.explanation: Central/primary = most painful, at the innervation point ("knot"). Satellites form in the referral zone of a central TrP. (TrP Part 1)

questions.q: Satellite trigger points usually:
options: Do not respond until the primary trigger point is treated
questions.explanation: Satellites form in response to a central TrP within its referral zone; treat the primary first. (TrP Part 1)

questions.q: A latent trigger point:
options: Feels like a TrP but is not painful and does not refer on palpation
Is always the most painful point
questions.explanation: Latent TrPs are not painful/referring but can become active after injury or if their primary activates. (TrP Part 1)

questions.q: Which classic theory explains trigger points through muscle spindles?
options: A sensitised spindle fires continuously and does not let the fibre lengthen, forming a spasm
Spindles release lymph into the muscle
questions.explanation: Muscle-spindle theory: sensitised spindle (injury, overload, sustained contraction) → continuous firing → spasm/TrP. (TrP Part 2)

questions.q: Ziembicki (2023) proposed that trigger points are located at:
options: Nerve Entry Points along the course of a nerve
questions.explanation: Myofascial TrPs connect to distinct points along a nerve (NEPs) – anatomical basis. (TrP Part 2)

questions.q: Quintner and Cohen's critique (1994) suggested referred pain in "trigger points" may come from:
options: Peripheral nerve irritation rather than an injury in muscle tissue
questions.explanation: They proposed peripheral neural irritation/inflammation or ischaemia; modern reviews use a multifactorial model. (TrP Part 1–2)

questions.q: Wolfe et al. (1992) found that:
options: Even leading experts cannot reliably locate trigger points
Trigger points are always harder on algometry
questions.explanation: Experts could not accurately and reliably locate TrPs. Andersen 2010 found the "hard" spots were softer on algometry. (TrP Part 2)

questions.q: Sprenger et al. (2011) attribute pain reduction after painful treatments such as dry needling to:
options: Diffuse noxious inhibitory control plus expectation and placebo
questions.explanation: DNIC and non-specific psychological effects (expectation, placebo). (TrP Part 2)

questions.q: Which autonomic change is "pilomotor"?
questions.explanation: Sudomotor = sweaty/shiny skin; vasomotor = circulation; pilomotor = hair loss/gain, goosebumps. (TrP Part 1)

questions.q: During manual pressure release, the patient's pain on the NRS should be no more than:
questions.explanation: Moderate pressure; pain no more than 5–6/10. (TrP Part 1)

questions.q: What is the maximum hold time for trigger-point pressure in the course method?
options: 10 seconds or until the pain eases
questions.explanation: Maintain pressure until pain eases, maximum 10 s, then rest and repeat about 3 times (2–4). (TrP Part 1)

questions.q: When should you stop trigger-point pressure?
questions.explanation: "Stop if the pain increases!!!" (TrP short version)

questions.q: Which is listed as a PRECAUTION (not a contraindication) for trigger-point therapy?
questions.explanation: Precautions: high pain, hypersensitivity, anxiety, acute healing, pregnancy, epilepsy, anticoagulants. Malignancy, open wounds and recent burns are contraindications. (TrP Part 1)

questions.q: Lew et al. (2021) meta-analysis compared dry needling with trigger-point manual therapy for neck/upper-back pain and found:
options: They were equal for VAS, PPT and NDI in the short to medium term
questions.explanation: DN and TrP manual therapy were equal. (TrP Part 1 / study pack)

questions.q: Zhou et al. (2023) found that adding which component to clinical TrP treatment gave better pain, ROM and function?
questions.explanation: Adding exercise improves outcomes more than a single treatment. (TrP Part 1)

questions.q: The most common sites for trigger-point injections listed in the slides include:
options: Masseter, levator scapulae, gluteus medius, QL, trapezius, SCM, temporalis
questions.explanation: Hammi et al. 2023 list. (TrP Part 2)

questions.q: The piriformis is called a "double devil" (Travell & Simons) because it:
options: Causes distress both by nerve entrapment and by projecting pain from trigger points
questions.explanation: Quote in TrP Part 2; Lewis 2016 found the sciatic nerve passed beneath piriformis in 89% of limbs. (TrP Part 2)

questions.q: The Mulligan concept was developed by:
options: Brian Mulligan, a New Zealand physiotherapist
questions.explanation: Brian Mulligan (NZ), influenced mainly by Kaltenborn; taught internationally from 1972. (Mulligan lecture)

questions.q: Mulligan's core idea is that pain is related to:
questions.explanation: Key idea: "positional faults". (Mulligan lecture)

questions.q: A Mobilisation With Movement combines:
options: A therapist-applied accessory glide with a patient-generated active movement
A passive physiological movement at end range
questions.explanation: MWM = therapist joint mobilisation + patient active movement to achieve pain-free function. (Mulligan lecture)

questions.q: What does the PILL response stand for?
questions.explanation: If there is no PILL response you do not use the technique. (Mulligan lecture)

questions.q: In the CROCKS rules, how many repetitions are suggested?
questions.explanation: CROCKS: Contraindications, Repetitions (3–10), Overpressure, Communication, Knowledge, Sustain. (Mulligan lecture)

questions.q: What is a "comparable sign"?
options: A reproducible movement, position or activity that brings on the symptoms and can be retested after treatment
A sign on the opposite limb
The patient's pain score at rest only
questions.explanation: Also called asterisk sign(*). (Mulligan lecture)

questions.q: What does SNAG stand for?
questions.explanation: NAGs = natural apophyseal glides; SNAGs = sustained; MWMs = mobilisation with movement; SMWAMs/SMWLMs = spinal with arm/leg movement. (Mulligan lecture)

questions.q: If an MWM is ineffective after a few repetitions (3–6), you should:
options: Stop, re-examine or abandon the technique
questions.explanation: Practical safety tips. (Mulligan lecture)

questions.q: For lateral epicondylalgia, the Mulligan lateral glide is applied while the patient:
options: Grips a dynamometer or rolled towel
Lies prone with the elbow straight and relaxed
questions.explanation: Lateral glide of the proximal ulna while gripping; pain must reduce by ≥50%. (Mulligan lecture)

questions.q: For the elbow lateral glide to be used as treatment, pain must reduce by at least:
questions.explanation: Pain must reduce by at least 50%; it is both test and treatment. (Mulligan lecture)

questions.q: Mulligan's general rule for knee MWM glide direction is:
options: Lateral glide for lateral knee pain, medial glide for medial knee pain
Opposite glide to the painful side
questions.explanation: Knee flexion with lateral/medial glide. (Mulligan lecture)

questions.q: Bisset et al. (2006) found that MWM plus exercise for tennis elbow was superior to:
questions.explanation: Bisset 2006 BMJ RCT. (Mulligan lecture)

questions.q: The Mulligan talocrural MWM for restricted dorsiflexion is performed:
options: In weight bearing (lunge) with a glide through the tibia/fibula
Prone with the knee flexed and no movement
Supine with the ankle in full plantarflexion
Sitting with the foot off the floor
questions.explanation: Patient in a weight-bearing lunge; glide applied as patient dorsiflexes. (Mulligan lecture)

questions.q: Mulligan contraindications are essentially the same as those for:
questions.explanation: Fracture, malignancy, open wounds, acute injury/post-op; precautions: hypermobility, osteoporosis, irritable pain, poor comprehension. (Mulligan lecture)

questions.q: Evidence for MWMs is strongest for which conditions?
options: Lateral epicondylalgia, post-sprain dorsiflexion restriction, knee OA and shoulder pain
questions.explanation: Mostly short- to medium-term benefits. Pourahmadi 2018 found insufficient evidence for LBP. (Mulligan lecture)

questions.q: Who developed Muscle Energy Technique, and when?
questions.explanation: MET is an osteopathic technique developed by Fred Mitchell Sr in 1948. (MET lecture)

questions.q: MET is defined as a direct manipulative procedure using:
options: A voluntary contraction of the patient's muscles against a distinctly controlled counterforce
A high-velocity thrust by the therapist
questions.explanation: Voluntary contraction against controlled counterforce from a precise position and in a specific direction. (MET lecture)

questions.q: Post-isometric relaxation (PIR) is based on:
options: Autogenic inhibition – contracting then stretching the same muscle
questions.explanation: PIR = contract-relax of the same muscle (autogenic inhibition). (MET lecture)

questions.q: In reciprocal inhibition MET, the patient contracts:
options: The opposing muscle, which relaxes the target muscle that is then stretched
questions.explanation: Contracting a muscle forces its reciprocal (opposing) muscle to relax. (MET lecture)

questions.q: Which receptors are activated during an isometric contraction and produce autogenic inhibition?
questions.explanation: GTOs respond to tension; 1b fibres stimulate inhibitory neurons. (MET lecture)

questions.q: In the course PIR protocol, how long does the therapist resist the isometric contraction?
questions.explanation: Counterforce 7–10 s, relax 3–5 s, take up slack to new barrier, repeat 2–4 times. (MET lecture)

questions.q: Which is a COMMON MET error highlighted in the slides?
options: The therapist re-engages a new barrier
questions.explanation: Errors: too far into barrier, patient pushes too hard, contraction too short, too few reps, movement allowed, unstable support, poor positioning. (MET lecture)

questions.q: Which is a specific contraindication to MET?
questions.explanation: Fracture, dislocation/instability, patient unable to understand or uncooperative. (MET lecture)

questions.q: How does MET differ from static stretching?
options: MET uses an isometric contraction and is not usually performed at full end range
MET holds the stretch at greatest length for 60 s with no contraction
questions.explanation: Static stretching has no contraction and is held at greatest length (15–60 s). (MET lecture)

questions.q: The iliopsoas MET is performed in which test position?
questions.explanation: Thomas test position; untreated leg fully flexed to stabilise lumbar spine. (MET lecture)

questions.q: In the Thomas test position, adding knee flexion localises the stretch to:
questions.explanation: Abduction → pectineus/short adductors; adduction → TFL; knee flexion → rectus femoris. (MET lecture)

questions.q: Why is MET often preferred over trigger-point therapy for subscapularis and iliopsoas?
options: They are difficult muscles to trigger-point
questions.explanation: Both described as difficult muscles to apply TrP therapy to. (MET lecture)

questions.q: Research patterns for MET show that it:
options: Works better as an adjunct, mostly with short-term effects
Has strong long-term evidence as a standalone treatment
Is harmful in low back pain
Has never been studied in RCTs
questions.explanation: Adjunct use better; immediate/short-term benefits; heterogeneous, small studies. (MET lecture)

questions.q: Kang/Yang et al. (2023) meta-analysis concluded MET for hamstring flexibility is:
options: More effective than no treatment and somewhat better than simple stretching
questions.explanation: 19 studies; risk of bias noted. (MET lecture)

questions.q: Myofascial release involves:
options: Low-load, long-duration mechanical forces to the myofascial complex
Very light skin stretching towards lymph nodes
questions.explanation: Barnes 1990: aims to restore optimum length, decrease pain and improve function. (MFR lecture)

questions.q: What is the primary cell type of fascia?
questions.explanation: Fibroblasts adapt to mechanical loading; MFR directs force to them. (MFR lecture)

questions.q: Superficial fascia (hypodermis) is found:
options: Between skin and muscles and contains adipose tissue
questions.explanation: Deep fascia is between adjacent muscles. (MFR lecture)

questions.q: "Anatomy trains" (Myers) propose that:
options: Tension in one part of a fascial line may decrease flexibility globally
Bones are connected by trains of ligaments only
questions.explanation: A schematic map of fascial connections. (MFR lecture)

questions.q: The SIN factor stands for:
questions.explanation: Gained from the subjective assessment and used to guide treatment. (MFR lecture)

questions.q: To differentiate articular from myofascial neck limitation, the therapist lifts the patient's arms; if rotation increases, the source is:
questions.explanation: Increase = neuromyofascial; no change = articular. (MFR lecture)

questions.q: How should myofascial release techniques generally be applied?
options: Very slowly, with broad contact, aiming to disrupt the fascial layers
questions.explanation: Don't always use oil; transverse or longitudinal; flat hands/knuckles; very slow. (MFR lecture)

questions.q: The "pin and stretch" technique means:
options: Fixing a specific point in a muscle while the patient moves that muscle
questions.explanation: Tissues distal to the pin are affected (e.g. subscapularis with lateral rotation). (MFR lecture)

questions.q: Wiewelhove et al. (2019) meta-analysis suggested foam rolling is best justified as:
options: A warm-up activity rather than a recovery tool
A recovery tool rather than warm-up
questions.explanation: Healey 2014: no effect on performance; Junker & Stoggl 2015: lengthens hamstrings. (MFR lecture)

questions.q: Kasahara et al. (2023) found that 30 s static stretching, unlike foam rolling:
questions.explanation: FR recommended to increase ROM without decreasing MVC-ISO strength. (MFR lecture)

questions.q: Kidd (2009) argued MFR can never be evidence-based because:
options: It relies on the clinician–patient interaction and cannot be neutral
questions.explanation: Inter-rater reliability also low. (MFR lecture)

questions.q: When performing SCM myofascial release, the key safety warning is:
questions.explanation: Knuckles against anterior border of SCM while patient rotates away. (MFR lecture)

questions.q: Lymph forms mainly because of:
options: The pressure difference between the interstitium and lymphatic capillaries (hydrostatic and oncotic)
Active pumping by the heart into lymph nodes
questions.explanation: Hydrostatic and oncotic pressures. (MLD lecture)

questions.q: Lymphangions pulsate at an average frequency of about:
questions.explanation: Valve segments acting like "lymph hearts". (MLD lecture)

questions.q: The right upper quadrant of the body drains via the:
options: Right lymphatic duct into the right venous angle
Thoracic duct into the left venous angle
questions.explanation: Below diaphragm and left upper quadrant → thoracic duct → left venous angle. (MLD lecture)

questions.q: Low-volume (mechanical) insufficiency of the lymphatic system results in:
options: Lymphoedema, because transport capacity falls below normal load
Oedema with normal transport capacity overloaded
questions.explanation: High-volume (dynamic): normal capacity overwhelmed. Low-volume (mechanical): reduced capacity → lymphoedema. Safety valve: both. (MLD lecture)

questions.q: Up to what proportion of breast cancer patients undergoing axillary node dissection and radiation develop lymphoedema?
questions.explanation: Shih et al. 2009 – up to 50%. (MLD lecture)

questions.q: Who refined MLD in 1936?
questions.explanation: First introduced by Taylor Still in the late 1800s, refined by Vodder in 1936. (MLD lecture)

questions.q: Which hand movements belong to the Vodder method?
options: Pump, scoop, rotary, stationary circle, thumb circle
questions.explanation: Vodder strokes; Földi adds thrust/relaxation phases; Leduc uses call-up and reabsorption. (MLD lecture)

questions.q: MLD movements are characterised by:
options: Very low pressure with skin stretching, slow and repetitive, usually without oil
questions.explanation: Slow, repetitive, soporific; aim to avoid increasing capillary filtration. (MLD lecture)

questions.q: The MLD sequence starts:
options: Proximally and centrally (often the neck), clearing nodes before distal areas
questions.explanation: Proximal before distal; e.g. LL starts at inguinal nodes. (MLD lecture)

questions.q: In the Leduc sequence, the "call-up" manoeuvre:
options: Starts at the lymph nodes and progresses distally to stimulate lymph flow
Is applied directly over fibrosis to break it down
Is a deep pump at the heart
Is a stretch of the muscle
questions.explanation: Reabsorption manoeuvre is applied over the oedematous region. (MLD lecture)

questions.q: The course MLD sequence uses how many pumping manoeuvres on the ganglia?
questions.explanation: 10 pumping to ganglions, 5 call-up, 5 reabsorption, proximal to distal. (MLD lecture)

questions.q: Which is an ABSOLUTE contraindication to MLD?
questions.explanation: Absolute: acute inflammation, malignant tumours, DVT, major heart problems. The others are relative. (MLD lecture)

questions.q: Which is a RELATIVE contraindication to MLD?
questions.explanation: Relative: kidney problems, asthma, thyroid, medications, chemotherapy, 1st trimester, removed spleen, menstruation. (MLD lecture)

questions.q: Which is an indication for MLD?
questions.explanation: Lymphoedemas, post-op/post-traumatic, cyclic oedemas, pre/post plastic surgery. (MLD lecture)

questions.q: Which scar rises above skin level AND projects beyond the original wound margins?
questions.explanation: Hypertrophic stays within boundaries (4–8 weeks post-injury, rarely recurs); keloid extends beyond, can appear years later, often recurs. (Scars lecture)

questions.q: Hypertrophic scars occur in up to what proportion of burn injuries?
questions.explanation: 40–70% after surgery, up to 91% after burns. (Scars lecture)

questions.q: A 2nd degree burn is characterised by:
questions.explanation: 1st reddening; 2nd blistering; 3rd deep damage with full-thickness necrosis. (Scars lecture)

questions.q: A burn involving more than what percentage of body surface is considered serious (rule of nines)?
questions.explanation: Rule of nines slide. (Scars lecture)

questions.q: The correct order of wound healing stages is:
questions.explanation: Van Onselen 2018. (Scars lecture)

questions.q: How long does the maturation/remodelling phase last?
questions.explanation: Haemostasis hours; inflammation first 2 weeks; proliferation 2–6 weeks; maturation 12–24 months. (Scars lecture)

questions.q: You should NEVER massage directly on:
questions.explanation: Contraindications: keloid, cutaneous fragility, open wounds, infection, severe pain/inflammation. (Scars lecture)

questions.q: Scar massage generally begins:
options: After suture removal/wound healing – in rehab generally 2 weeks post-healing
Immediately after surgery on the open wound
questions.explanation: Scar must be fully closed with no scabbing; at least 10 min daily. (Scars lecture)

questions.q: If you plan friction or skin-rolling techniques on a scar, the lubricant should be applied:
questions.explanation: Tip from the scar lecture. (Scars lecture)

questions.q: Which effect of scar/burn massage is supported by good evidence in burns patients?
options: Reduced pain, itch, anxiety and depression
questions.explanation: Field 2000, Roh 2007; evidence for scar improvement remains inconsistent (Lin 2023). (Scars lecture)

questions.q: When a scar becomes inflamed during treatment you should:
questions.explanation: Considerations during treatment. Contractures/adhesions → more vigorous massage. (Scars lecture)

questions.q: The WHO (2007) defines cupping as:
options: A therapeutic method involving suction by creating a vacuum
Sustained pressure on a trigger point
questions.explanation: Mehta & Dhapte 2015: subatmospheric pressure by heat or suction. (Cupping lecture)

questions.q: In TCM, "sha" refers to:
options: Reddish, elevated, millet-like skin rashes brought to the surface
questions.explanation: "Gua" means to scrape; gua sha and cupping bring sha to the surface. (Cupping lecture)

questions.q: Strong cupping should be left in place for a maximum of:
questions.explanation: Not for weak, elderly or paediatric patients; always massage after; never on abdomen. (Cupping lecture)

questions.q: "Empty/flash" cupping means:
options: Strong cupping retained for less than 1 minute
questions.explanation: Used for drawing out a pathogen, e.g. start of a cold. (Cupping lecture)

questions.q: Which area should NEVER receive moving cupping?
questions.explanation: Medium cupping may be used on abdomen but never moving cupping. (Cupping lecture)

questions.q: How often is cupping usually effective for MSK disorders in the West?
options: Once a week (fortnightly if considerable marking)
questions.explanation: Don't repeat until bruising has disappeared. (Cupping lecture)

questions.q: Which is an ABSOLUTE contraindication to cupping?
questions.explanation: Absolute: cancer, organ failure, pacemaker, haemophilia, anticoagulants. (Cupping lecture)

questions.q: Mohammed et al. (2023) systematic review found moderate evidence for cupping in:
questions.explanation: Low-moderate for LBP/neck pain; adverse events very low. (Cupping lecture)

questions.q: Which adverse event is listed as NON-preventable?
questions.explanation: Aboushanab & AlSanad 2018 classification. (Cupping lecture)

questions.q: Cupping to the neck has been linked to which serious adverse effect?
options: Haemorrhagic stroke from an acute rise in blood pressure
questions.explanation: Chen et al. 2014. (Cupping lecture)

classes.title: Pathology of Trauma
classes.desc: Orthopaedic trauma by region, fracture management, imaging

questions.q: According to the lecture, who published "L'Orthopédie" (1741), the origin of the term orthopaedics?
questions.explanation: Nicolas Andry (1658–1742), professor at the Royal College in Paris, published L'Orthopédie in 1741. He did not practise surgery. (Lecture 1)

questions.q: The word "orthopaedics" combines the Greek "orthon" with "paidion". What do they mean?
questions.explanation: Orthon = straight/correct, paidion = children. (Lecture 1)

questions.q: Which term means a DEGENERATIVE tendon process?
questions.explanation: Tendinitis = inflammatory process in the tendon; tendinosis = degenerative process; tenosynovitis = inflammation of the synovial sheath; enthesitis = inflammation at the insertion point. (Lecture 1)

questions.q: Inflammation of the synovial membrane that covers a tendon is called:
questions.explanation: Tenosynovitis = inflammatory process of the synovial membrane covering the tendon. Synovitis refers to the joint synovium. (Lecture 1)

questions.q: An inflammatory process located at the insertion point of a muscle is called:
questions.explanation: Enthesitis ("entesite") = inflammation located at the muscle insertion point. (Lecture 1)

questions.q: Which term describes an infectious process of bone tissue?
questions.explanation: Osteomyelitis = infection of bone; pyoarthritis = joint infection; osteoarthritis = degenerative joint process. (Lecture 1)

questions.q: Pathological fusion of a joint is called:
questions.explanation: Ankylosis = pathological fusion. Arthrodesis is the SURGICAL fixation of a joint. (Lecture 1)

questions.q: How does the lecture define a dislocation?
options: Complete and persistent loss of contact between the joint surfaces
Partial loss of contact with partial congruence
A ligament injury from excessive stress with momentary subluxation
Loss of contact plus fracture of the adjacent bones
questions.explanation: Dislocation = complete, persistent loss of contact between joint surfaces. Partial loss = subluxation; with fractured adjacent bones = fracture-dislocation. (Lecture 1)

questions.q: "Partial loss of contact of joint surfaces, with partial congruence" defines:
questions.explanation: Subluxation = partial loss of contact; capsular and ligament injuries are less severe. (Lecture 1)

questions.q: Consolidation of a fracture with defective alignment is called:
questions.explanation: Malunion/vicious union = healed in bad alignment. Pseudoarthrosis = non-consolidation with instability at the fracture site. (Lecture 1)

questions.q: Pseudoarthrosis is best defined as:
options: Non-consolidation of a fracture with instability at the fracture site
Healing of a fracture in poor alignment
questions.explanation: Pseudoarthrosis = non-consolidation of a fracture characterised by instability of the fracture focus. (Lecture 1)

questions.q: Death of the cells of bone and bone marrow caused by ischaemia is:
questions.explanation: Avascular necrosis = death of the cellular component of bone and marrow resulting from ischaemia. (Lecture 1)

questions.q: Which tendon surgery converts a tendon into a ligament to stabilise an unstable joint?
questions.explanation: Tenodesis converts a tendon into a ligament (e.g. extensor hallucis tendon fixed to the 1st metatarsal neck). Tenotomy cuts a tendon; tenolysis releases a fibrous tunnel; transfer changes the insertion. (Lecture 1)

questions.q: Release of a fibrous tunnel after trauma (e.g. trigger finger) is called:
questions.explanation: Tenolysis = release of a fibrous tunnel, e.g. trigger finger. (Lecture 1)

questions.q: Moving the insertion of tibialis anterior to compensate for a fibular nerve lesion is an example of:
questions.explanation: Tendon transfer = exchange of insertion (e.g. anterior tibial for posterior in a fibular nerve lesion). (Lecture 1)

questions.q: Union of unstable fractures with metal implants is called:
questions.explanation: Osteosynthesis = union of unstable fractures using metal implants. Osteotomy = removal of a bone portion to correct deviations. (Lecture 1)

questions.q: A bone graft taken from another person is called:
questions.explanation: Autograft = from the same patient; allograft = from another person; xenograft = from another species. (Lecture 1)

questions.q: On a plain X-ray, which density appears BLACK?
questions.explanation: Gas = black (least absorption, e.g. lungs); fat = dark grey; water = light grey; calcium = white; metal = opaque white. (Lecture 1)

questions.q: On X-ray, muscles and viscera have which density?
questions.explanation: Water density (muscles, viscera) appears light grey. (Lecture 1)

questions.q: In the oblique-view "Scottie dog" sign of the lumbar spine, the pars interarticularis forms the dog's:
questions.explanation: Transverse process = nose, pedicle = eye, inferior facet = front leg, superior facet = ear, pars interarticularis = neck. (Lectures 1 & 8)

questions.q: In the Scottie dog sign, the pedicle represents the:
questions.explanation: Pedicle = eye; transverse process = nose. (Lecture 1)

questions.q: What is the main DISADVANTAGE of a CT scan listed in the lecture?
questions.explanation: CT gives high-contrast, cross-sectional and 3D images without superimposition, but its disadvantage is high radiation exposure. (Lecture 1)

questions.q: Bone scintigraphy shows abnormalities as "hot spots" because:
options: The radioactive tracer is taken up by metabolically active bone
Metal implants reflect the magnetic field
questions.explanation: A radioactive substance injected IV is taken up by metabolically active bone; increased metabolism appears as hot spots on a gamma camera. (Lecture 1, Seidenberg & Howe 2014)

questions.q: MRI is contraindicated in patients with:
questions.explanation: Because of the magnetic field MRI is contraindicated with pacemakers, defibrillators and spinal stimulators. (Lecture 1)

questions.q: Which pair of imaging techniques does NOT use ionising radiation?
questions.explanation: X-ray, CT and bone scintigraphy use ionising radiation; MRI and ultrasound do not. (Lecture 1 summary)

questions.q: Which imaging method can evaluate structures DYNAMICALLY at relatively low cost and without radiation?
questions.explanation: Musculoskeletal ultrasound uses sound waves, has no radiation risk, is low cost and can evaluate structures dynamically. (Lecture 1)

questions.q: A muscle strain is defined in the lecture as:
options: An acute or chronic injury of contractile components (muscles and tendons)
Damage to one or more ligaments of a joint
A haematoma caused by damaged capillaries
A fracture of a muscle insertion
questions.explanation: Strain (muscle tear/pulled muscle) = injury of contractile components; sprain = ligament damage; contusion = bruise. (Lecture 2)

questions.q: A sprain is damage to:
options: One or more ligaments of a joint
questions.explanation: Sprain = ligament damage when the joint is taken beyond its functional range. (Lecture 2)

questions.q: Which strain grade presents with NO movement and severe pain?
questions.explanation: First degree = little tearing, pain with full ROM; second = torn tissue, painful limited motion; third = most severe, no movement. (Lecture 2)

questions.q: Which list contains skeletal functions given in the lecture?
options: Support, movement, protection, mineral reserve, haemopoiesis
questions.explanation: Support, movement (through joints), protection, mineral reserve and haemopoiesis. (Lecture 2)

questions.q: Which fracture sign "should NOT be researched" (tested) according to the lecture?
questions.explanation: Abnormal mobility is a fracture sign that should not be provoked during examination. (Lecture 2)

questions.q: The absence of a history of trauma:
questions.explanation: Fatigue or pathological (e.g. osteoporotic) fractures occur without aggression – absence of trauma does NOT exclude fracture. (Lecture 2)

questions.q: A closed fracture that is complicated by significant soft-tissue injury is correctly termed:
questions.explanation: Open = compound (skin breached). A closed fracture complicated by soft-tissue injury = complex fracture. (Lecture 2)

questions.q: Which fracture patterns does the lecture list as UNSTABLE?
options: Oblique, spiral, comminuted or double fractures
questions.explanation: Stable: incomplete and transverse (held by muscle elastic contraction after reduction). Unstable: oblique, spiral, comminuted or double. (Lecture 2)

questions.q: Displacement of a fracture is described by the position of:
options: The distal fragment relative to the proximal bone
The proximal fragment relative to the distal bone
The fracture line relative to the joint
The bone relative to the skin
questions.explanation: Displacement is defined by the abnormal position of the distal fragment in relation to the proximal bone. (Lecture 2)

questions.q: A fracture in which one fragment is driven into another (e.g. distal radius) is:
questions.explanation: Impacted fracture = a bone fragment driven into another fragment. (Lecture 2)

questions.q: Why do intra-articular fractures matter?
options: They heal faster than diaphyseal fractures
questions.explanation: The lecture notes intra-articular fractures carry a risk of post-traumatic OA. (Lecture 2)

questions.q: Which two factors influence the time of fracture consolidation?
questions.explanation: There are no strict rules; the mechanical aspect (stability) and biological aspect (vascularisation) influence consolidation. (Lecture 2)

questions.q: The main difference between osteitis and osteomyelitis is that osteomyelitis spreads:
options: Centrifugally, starting as an infection of the bone marrow
Centripetally, from the soft tissue inward
questions.explanation: Osteitis = centripetal; osteomyelitis = centrifugal (primary infection of the bone marrow, then cortex and periosteum). (Lecture 2)

questions.q: In compartment syndrome, the FIRST pathogenic event is:
options: Tissue pressure exceeds venous pressure, impairing outflow
questions.explanation: Sequence: tissue pressure > venous pressure → arterial compromise → neural/muscle dysfunction → ischaemic necrosis/contracture → (severe) renal failure & death. (Lecture 2)

questions.q: After roughly how long without blood supply does progressive muscle necrosis begin in compartment syndrome?
questions.explanation: Muscle tolerates short periods of hypoxia but after a few hours (6–8 h) progressive necrosis begins. (Lecture 2)

questions.q: What is the treatment of compartment syndrome?
questions.explanation: Treatment = release of the closed osteofascial compartment by surgical dermatofasciotomy. (Lectures 2 & 11)

questions.q: Torus (buckle) fractures typically involve:
options: The distal radial metaphysis in children after a fall on an outstretched arm
The femoral neck in the elderly
The fifth metatarsal neck after punching
questions.explanation: Torus/buckle fractures = incomplete fractures with cortical bulging from axial loading, frequently the distal radial metaphysis in children. (Lecture 2)

questions.q: Physeal (growth plate) fractures make up what proportion of children's fractures?
questions.explanation: Physeal fractures are common, 15–30% of all fractures in children. (Lecture 2)

questions.q: An insufficiency fracture occurs when:
options: Osteoporotic bone is subjected to normal stress
Normal bone is subjected to abnormal activity
A muscle avulses a bony fragment
questions.explanation: Insufficiency fracture = abnormal (osteoporotic) bone + normal stress; stress/fatigue fracture = normal bone + abnormal activity (overuse). (Lecture 2)

questions.q: The most common sites of stress fractures in the foot are the:
questions.explanation: The 2nd and 3rd metatarsals (greatest impact during push-off). (Lecture 2)

questions.q: Tibial stress fractures in runners account for up to:
questions.explanation: Tibial stress fractures are a common overuse injury in runners, accounting for up to half of all stress fractures. (Lecture 2)

questions.q: The "female athlete triad" associated with stress fractures consists of:
questions.explanation: A stress fracture may herald underlying amenorrhoea, disordered eating and osteoporosis. (Lecture 2)

questions.q: The main management of most stress fractures is:
questions.explanation: Most stress fractures are managed conservatively with rest; high-risk displaced ones need surgery. (Lecture 2)

questions.q: Which rotator cuff muscle is the most commonly ruptured?
questions.explanation: SITS muscles; supraspinatus is the most commonly ruptured. (Lecture 3)

questions.q: Most clavicle fractures (94%) result from:
options: A direct blow on the shoulder, generally a fall on the side
A fall on an outstretched hand
A twisting injury of the arm
questions.explanation: 94% result from a direct blow on the shoulder, generally falling on the side. (Lecture 3, McRae)

questions.q: Why are fractures of the middle third of the clavicle most common?
options: It is the thinnest part and not reinforced by muscles or ligaments
It is the thickest part of the bone
It is where the growth plate is located
questions.explanation: The middle is the thinnest part and the only part not reinforced by muscles and ligaments. (Lecture 3)

questions.q: In adults, the medial fragment of a displaced clavicle fracture is pulled upward by:
questions.explanation: Weight of the limb pulls the distal fragment down; SCM pulls the medial fragment up. (Lecture 3)

questions.q: According to the AAOS guidance in the lecture, displaced midshaft clavicle fractures in adults:
options: Should always be treated with a figure-of-eight brace
questions.explanation: Displaced midshaft (adults): surgical fixation recommended (higher union, better early outcomes). Simple sling preferred over figure-of-eight; LIPUS not recommended. (Lecture 3)

questions.q: In the Neer classification, a "part" is considered displaced if there is:
questions.explanation: Neer: displaced part = >1 cm separation or >45° angulation. (Lecture 3)

questions.q: Which Neer category accounts for about 75% of proximal humerus fractures?
questions.explanation: One-part ~75%, two-part ~20%, three-part ~5%, four-part <1%. (Lecture 3)

questions.q: Which proximal humerus fracture type carries a high risk of avascular necrosis?
questions.explanation: Four-part: all parts displaced, articular surface lateral and out of contact with glenoid – high AVN risk. (Lecture 3)

questions.q: What are Codman's four "parts" of the proximal humerus?
options: Articular surface, greater tuberosity, lesser tuberosity, humeral shaft
Anatomical neck, surgical neck, shaft, epicondyle
questions.explanation: Articular surface, greater tuberosity, lesser tuberosity and shaft. (Lecture 3)

questions.q: For an elderly, active patient with a displaced 3- or 4-part proximal humerus fracture, the lecture suggests:
questions.explanation: Decision summary: young/fit → ORIF; elderly active → RSA; frail/low demand → conservative. (Lecture 3)

questions.q: Which nerve is most commonly injured in humeral shaft fractures?
questions.explanation: The radial nerve runs in the spiral groove – the most common associated injury. Most recover in 3–6 months. (Lecture 3)

questions.q: Anterior proximal humerus fracture-dislocations may injure the:
questions.explanation: Anterior fracture-dislocations may injure the axillary nerve. (Lecture 3)

questions.q: Which joint suffers the most dislocations in the body?
questions.explanation: Shoulder = 45% of all dislocations; 84% anterior glenohumeral. (Lecture 3)

questions.q: In type III acromioclavicular dislocation:
options: The coracoclavicular (trapezoid and conoid) ligaments are ruptured
Only the AC ligament is sprained
questions.explanation: Type I = sprain; Type II = AC ligament torn + CC sprain; Type III = CC ligaments ruptured. (Lecture 3)

questions.q: Which is a DYNAMIC shoulder stabiliser?
questions.explanation: Static: capsular ligaments, labrum, negative pressure. Dynamic: rotator cuff, long head of biceps, deltoid, pectoralis major. (Lecture 3)

questions.q: The acronym TUBS stands for:
questions.explanation: TUBS = Traumatic Unidirectional Bankart Surgery; first episode usually anterior. (Lecture 3)

questions.q: The acronym AMBRI describes instability that is:
options: Atraumatic, Multidirectional, Bilateral, treated with Rehabilitation, Inferior capsular shift
questions.explanation: AMBRI – mostly due to laxity; good prognosis with conservative rehabilitation. (Lecture 3)

questions.q: A Hill-Sachs lesion is:
options: A posterolateral humeral head compression fracture
A superior labral tear from anterior to posterior
questions.explanation: Hill-Sachs = posterolateral humeral head compression fracture; Bankart = anteroinferior labral detachment; SLAP = superior labrum. (Lecture 3)

questions.q: AIOS instability results from:
questions.explanation: AIOS = Acquired Instability Overstress (Surgery may be needed) – repetitive microtrauma in occupational/sports activities. (Lecture 3)

questions.q: Which muscle is MOST predominantly involved in tennis elbow?
questions.explanation: Lateral epicondylitis: ECRB most predominantly, also ECRL, extensor digitorum communis, ECU. (Lecture 4)

questions.q: What proportion of tennis elbow patients do NOT play sports?
questions.explanation: High incidence (35–55 y); 95% of patients do not practise sports. (Lecture 4)

questions.q: Golfer's elbow pain is aggravated by:
questions.explanation: Medial epicondylitis is aggravated by resisted wrist flexion and pronation. (Lecture 4)

questions.q: Pathophysiologically, epicondylitis is described as:
options: A chronic tendinosis with disorganised tissue and neovessels
questions.explanation: Epicondylitis represents a chronic tendinosis rather than an acute inflammatory process. (Lecture 4)

questions.q: What percentage of epicondylitis cases can be managed non-operatively?
questions.explanation: Over 90%; surgery only after ≥6 months of failed non-operative care. Eccentric strengthening is effective. (Lecture 4)

questions.q: Counterforce braces for epicondylitis are placed approximately:
options: 6–10 cm distal to the elbow joint
questions.explanation: Placed on the forearm about 6–10 cm distal to the elbow joint. (Lecture 4)

questions.q: Cubital tunnel syndrome is entrapment of which nerve?
questions.explanation: The cubital tunnel lets the ulnar nerve pass from arm to forearm; paraesthesia in digits 4 and 5. (Lecture 4)

questions.q: The most common elbow fracture in children (peak 5–7 years) is:
questions.explanation: Supracondylar fracture – mechanism: fall on a hyperextended elbow. (Lecture 4)

questions.q: Volkmann's contracture after a supracondylar fracture is caused by:
options: Ischaemic injury to the brachial artery
questions.explanation: Volkmann's contracture = ischaemic injury of the brachial artery causing permanent flexion of hand and wrist. Cubitus varus (gunstock) is the malunion. (Lecture 4)

questions.q: The "gunstock deformity" after a supracondylar fracture is:
questions.explanation: Cubitus varus malunion = gunstock deformity. (Lecture 4)

questions.q: Radial head fractures constitute about what proportion of elbow fractures?
questions.explanation: 33%; mechanism: FOOSH with elbow extended and forearm pronated; often subtle on X-ray. (Lecture 4)

questions.q: A Mason type IV radial head fracture is:
options: A radial head fracture with associated elbow dislocation
questions.explanation: Mason I non-displaced; II partial >2 mm; III comminuted; IV with elbow dislocation. (Lecture 4)

questions.q: A Monteggia fracture is:
options: Fracture of the proximal/middle ulna with dislocation of the radial head
Fracture of the distal radius with DRUJ dislocation
Fracture of the radial head and coronoid with elbow dislocation
Transverse fracture of the 5th metacarpal neck
questions.explanation: Monteggia = ulna fracture + radial head dislocation (peak 4–10 y). Galeazzi = distal radius + DRUJ. (Lecture 4)

questions.q: The terrible triad of the elbow consists of:
options: Elbow dislocation + radial head fracture + coronoid fracture
Olecranon + radial head + ulnar nerve injury
Supracondylar fracture + brachial artery + median nerve injury
questions.explanation: Terrible triad = elbow dislocation, radial head fracture and coronoid fracture (often collateral ligament injury). (Lecture 4)

questions.q: The elbow is the most commonly dislocated joint in:
questions.explanation: Elbow dislocation = most common in children, second most common in adults; mostly posterolateral after FOOSH. (Lecture 4)

questions.q: Which fracture is the 3rd most common in children and associated with elbow dislocation in 50% of cases?
questions.explanation: Medial epicondyle fracture – 50% associated with elbow dislocation; caused by valgus avulsion. (Lecture 4)

questions.q: Carpal tunnel syndrome is entrapment of the:
questions.explanation: CTS = median nerve entrapment; tests: Phalen, reverse Phalen, Tinel, EMG/nerve conduction. (Lecture 5)

questions.q: De Quervain's tenosynovitis affects the tendons of:
options: Extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus
Flexor pollicis longus and flexor digitorum profundus
Extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis
questions.explanation: EPB and APL; tested with Finkelstein's and Eichhoff's tests. (Lecture 5)

questions.q: Dupuytren's contracture is:
questions.explanation: Fibrosis of the palmar fascia, mostly in people >50; nodule then cords. (Lecture 5)

questions.q: A Colles' fracture is:
options: Transverse distal radius fracture with DORSAL displacement after a fall on an outstretched hand
Distal radius fracture with ANTERIOR displacement after a fall on a flexed wrist
Distal radius fracture with DRUJ dislocation
Fracture at the base of the 1st metacarpal
questions.explanation: Colles' = dorsal deviation, "dinner fork" deformity, ulnar styloid fracture in >60%. Smith's = reverse (anterior). (Lecture 5)

questions.q: Smith's fracture results from:
options: A fall onto a flexed wrist, with anterior displacement
A fall onto an outstretched hand, with dorsal displacement
questions.explanation: Smith's (reverse Colles') = fall onto flexed wrist, anterior deviation; less common than Colles'. (Lecture 5)

questions.q: The most common carpal fracture is the:
questions.explanation: Scaphoid = most common (anatomical snuffbox tenderness); triquetrum = 2nd (15%). (Lecture 5)

questions.q: Which part of the scaphoid has the highest risk of non-union/AVN?
questions.explanation: Distal pole ~100% union; waist 10–20% non-union; proximal pole 30–40%. (Lecture 5)

questions.q: Kienböck's disease is avascular necrosis of the:
questions.explanation: Kienböck's = AVN of the lunate; negative ulnar variance may contribute. (Lecture 5)

questions.q: A Bennett fracture is:
options: An intra-articular two-part fracture-dislocation at the base of the 1st metacarpal
A comminuted (≥3 parts) fracture at the base of the 1st metacarpal
A transverse fracture of the 5th metacarpal neck
questions.explanation: Bennett = two-part; Rolando = comminuted (≥3 parts); both from forced abduction. (Lecture 5)

questions.q: A boxer's fracture is a fracture of the:
questions.explanation: Boxer's fracture = transverse fracture of the 5th metacarpal neck; most common metacarpal fracture. (Lecture 5)

questions.q: A Galeazzi fracture is:
options: Distal radius fracture with dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint
Proximal ulna fracture with radial head dislocation
Distal radius fracture with dorsal angulation only
questions.explanation: Galeazzi = distal radius + DRUJ dislocation (fall on outstretched hand with flexed elbow). (Lecture 5)

questions.q: How many vertebrae make up the cervical spine?
questions.explanation: 33 vertebrae: cervical 7, thoracic 12, lumbar 5, sacral 5 (fused), coccygeal 4 (fused). (Lecture 6)

questions.q: A normal cervical lordosis (C2–C7) measures:
questions.explanation: Normal 20–40°; hyperlordosis >40°; reversed ~0°. (Lecture 6)

questions.q: About 70% of cervical radiculopathy is caused by:
questions.explanation: 70% due to ageing degeneration (foramina, vertebral bodies, facets); disc herniation is less frequent. (Lecture 6)

questions.q: Whiplash-associated disorder results from:
options: Rapid hyperflexion–extension of the neck, without fracture
Direct blow to the vertebral arch
questions.explanation: WAD = rapid flexion–extension (car accidents); soft-tissue injury, managed conservatively in nearly all cases. (Lecture 6)

questions.q: Unilateral cervical facet dislocation causes roughly how much anterior vertebral displacement?
questions.explanation: Unilateral ≈25%; bilateral ≈50% (highly unstable, usually cord injury). (Lecture 6)

questions.q: A "stinger" injury involves:
options: Traction or compression of the brachial plexus (often C5–C6) causing transient symptoms
questions.explanation: Sudden lateral neck flexion with shoulder depression → transient burning pain down the arm. (Lecture 6)

questions.q: An atlantodental interval greater than what suggests atlantoaxial instability in adults?
questions.explanation: ADI >3 mm in adults on lateral X-ray. Causes include trauma, RA, Down syndrome. (Lecture 6)

questions.q: A Jefferson fracture is:
options: A burst fracture of the C1 ring from axial loading (e.g. diving into shallow water)
A fracture of the C2 dens
An avulsion of the C7 spinous process
questions.explanation: Burst fracture of the atlas (anterior and posterior arches). Stability depends on the transverse ligament. (Lecture 6)

questions.q: Which odontoid fracture type (Anderson & D'Alonzo) is the most common and unstable?
options: Type II – base of the dens
Type I – tip of the dens
Type III – into the C2 body
questions.explanation: Type I tip (rare, stable); Type II base (most common, unstable); Type III into body (moderate). (Lecture 6)

questions.q: Scheuermann's kyphosis is diagnosed when there is anterior wedging of:
options: Any wedging in the lumbar spine
questions.explanation: Thoracic kyphosis >40–45° Cobb plus anterior wedging ≥5° in ≥3 adjacent vertebrae; rigid (unlike postural kyphosis). (Lecture 7)

questions.q: Which feature distinguishes Scheuermann's kyphosis from postural kyphosis?
options: It is rigid and does not correct on extension
It is in the coronal plane
questions.explanation: Postural kyphosis is flexible; Scheuermann's is fixed. (Lecture 7)

questions.q: A Cobb angle of at least how many degrees is needed to diagnose scoliosis?
questions.explanation: ≥10° diagnosis; 10–20° mild; 20–40° moderate; >40° significant; >50° severe. (Lecture 7)

questions.q: The most common curve in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis is:
questions.explanation: Most common = right thoracic; atypical curves (e.g. left thoracic) warrant MRI. (Lecture 7)

questions.q: Bracing for AIS is indicated for curves of:
questions.explanation: <20–25° observe; 25–45° (Risser 0–2) brace; ≥45–50° surgery. (Lecture 7)

questions.q: A Risser grade 5 means:
options: Complete fusion of the iliac crest apophysis – skeletal maturity
questions.explanation: Risser 0 = no ossification (very high risk); 5 = complete fusion, growth complete, no bracing needed. (Lecture 7)

questions.q: In the Denis three-column model, the MIDDLE column includes:
options: Posterior half of the vertebral body and disc plus the posterior longitudinal ligament
Anterior longitudinal ligament and anterior half of the body
Facet joints, lamina and spinous process
questions.explanation: Anterior: ALL + anterior half of body/disc. Middle: posterior half + PLL. Posterior: facets, flavum, lamina, spinous process. (Lecture 7)

questions.q: A burst fracture involves failure of which columns?
questions.explanation: Burst = high-energy axial load; anterior and middle columns fail; common at T10–L2. (Lectures 7–8)

questions.q: A Chance (seat-belt) fracture is caused by:
questions.explanation: Lap belt fixes pelvis while the upper body flexes forward; horizontal fracture through body, pedicles and spinous process. (Lecture 7)

questions.q: Clay-shoveler's fracture is an avulsion of the:
options: Spinous process (usually C6, C7 or T1)
questions.explanation: Avulsion of the spinous process from forceful trapezius/rhomboid contraction; stable (posterior column only). (Lecture 7)

questions.q: Chronic low back pain is pain lasting more than:
questions.explanation: Acute <6 weeks; subacute 6–12 weeks; chronic >12 weeks. (Lecture 8)

questions.q: Approximately what proportion of low back pain is mechanical?
questions.explanation: Mechanical ≈90% (strain/sprain most common); non-mechanical ≈10%. (Lecture 8)

questions.q: Bowel or bladder dysfunction in a low back pain patient suggests:
options: Cauda equina syndrome – a red flag
questions.explanation: Bowel/bladder dysfunction is a red flag suggesting cauda equina syndrome. (Lecture 8)

questions.q: Lumbar disc herniation is most common at:
questions.explanation: Most common at L4–L5 and L5–S1. MRI = gold standard. (Lecture 8)

questions.q: An S1 root compression typically affects:
options: The posterior leg, plantar foot and Achilles reflex
The anterior thigh and knee reflex
The lateral leg and dorsal foot
questions.explanation: L4 → anterior thigh, knee reflex; L5 → lateral leg, dorsal foot; S1 → posterior leg, plantar foot, Achilles reflex. (Lecture 8)

questions.q: Spondylolysis is:
options: A defect/stress fracture of the pars interarticularis
questions.explanation: Pars defect, 90% at L5; from repetitive hyperextension. Spondylolisthesis = slippage. (Lecture 8)

questions.q: A Meyerding grade III spondylolisthesis corresponds to a slip of:
questions.explanation: I <25%; II 25–50%; III 50–75%; IV 75–100%; V >100% (spondyloptosis). (Lecture 8)

questions.q: In the Wiltse classification, isthmic spondylolisthesis is due to:
options: A pars interarticularis defect (stress fracture), common in young athletes
Excessive surgical removal of posterior elements
questions.explanation: Dysplastic = congenital; isthmic = pars defect; degenerative = facet OA; iatrogenic = laminectomy. (Lecture 8)

questions.q: Athletic pubalgia is mostly due to imbalance between which muscles at the pubis?
options: Adductors and abdominals (rectus abdominis vs adductor longus)
questions.explanation: Rectus abdominis and adductor longus pull in opposite directions; imbalance → groin pain. (Lecture 9)

questions.q: The imaging of choice to confirm a core muscle injury in athletic pubalgia is:
questions.explanation: MRI shows tears/oedema at tendon insertions and rules out other conditions. (Lecture 9)

questions.q: Piriformis syndrome pain is typically reproduced with the:
questions.explanation: FAIR test, resisted external rotation or passive internal rotation. (Lecture 9)

questions.q: Greater trochanteric pain syndrome is now known to involve mainly:
questions.explanation: Historically "trochanteric bursitis", now known to be mainly gluteal tendinopathy. (Lecture 9)

questions.q: A cam-type femoroacetabular impingement is:
options: An aspherical femoral head / bump at the head–neck junction
A labral tear without bony change
questions.explanation: Cam = aspherical head/bump; pincer = excessive acetabular coverage; most are mixed. (Lecture 9)

questions.q: The clinical test for FAI described in the lecture is:
questions.explanation: FADIR (+) = pain in flexion-adduction-internal rotation. (Lecture 9)

questions.q: The ASIS avulsion fracture in adolescent athletes is caused by which muscle?
questions.explanation: ASIS – sartorius; AIIS – rectus femoris; ischial tuberosity – hamstrings. (Lecture 9)

questions.q: Femoral neck fractures are classified with the:
questions.explanation: Garden I–IV; nondisplaced I–II → screws; displaced III–IV → hemiarthroplasty or THR. (Lecture 9)

questions.q: Which hip fracture has a HIGH risk of avascular necrosis?
questions.explanation: Intracapsular femoral neck fractures disrupt blood supply → high AVN risk. (Lecture 9)

questions.q: Surgery for hip fracture is recommended within:
questions.explanation: Timing 24–48 h (AAOS 2023). (Lecture 9)

questions.q: The mean age for hip fracture given in the lecture is:
questions.explanation: 90% occur above 65; mean age 80; females 2:1. (Lecture 9)

questions.q: What is the gold-standard surgical treatment for severe hip osteoarthritis?
questions.explanation: THA = gold standard; arthroscopy is not indicated for advanced OA. (Lecture 9)

questions.q: According to the lecture, using a cane in the OPPOSITE hand reduces hip joint load by about:
questions.explanation: Assistive device (cane in opposite hand) reduces load by ~30%. (Lecture 9)

questions.q: The "unhappy triad" (O'Donoghue's triad) involves:
questions.explanation: Injury to ACL, MCL and medial meniscus. (Lecture 10)

questions.q: Which knee ligament is most frequently injured?
questions.explanation: Ligament injuries = 40% of traumatic knee injuries; ACL most frequent. (Lecture 10)

questions.q: Which test is NOT used to examine the ACL?
questions.explanation: ACL: anterior drawer, Lachman, pivot shift. Posterior drawer and sag sign = PCL. (Lecture 10)

questions.q: A PCL "dashboard injury" is:
options: A direct blow to the proximal tibia with the knee flexed
Valgus with internal rotation during pivoting
A direct blow to the lateral knee
questions.explanation: Posteriorly directed force on a flexed knee (car accidents). (Lecture 10)

questions.q: An MCL sprain typically results from:
options: A direct blow to the LATERAL knee pushing it inwards
A direct blow to the medial knee pushing it outwards
questions.explanation: MCL: blow to lateral knee (valgus); LCL: blow to inside of the knee (varus). (Lecture 10)

questions.q: Which meniscus is more mobile and less liable to injury?
questions.explanation: Lateral: small, circular, more mobile, less liable. Medial: large, oval, attached to capsule and MCL, more liable. (Lecture 10)

questions.q: Which test is a meniscal test from the lecture?
questions.explanation: Meniscal tests: McMurray, Apley compression, Thessaly; MRI is standard. (Lecture 10)

questions.q: Pes anserinus is the combined insertion of:
options: Rectus femoris, vastus medialis and sartorius
questions.explanation: Sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus (≈5 cm distal to the medial knee). (Lecture 10)

questions.q: Iliotibial band syndrome is the second most common overuse knee pain after:
questions.explanation: ITBS – lateral knee overuse injury in runners; positive Noble compression test. (Lecture 10)

questions.q: Which hip-muscle weakness is linked to patellofemoral pain syndrome?
questions.explanation: Weakness of gluteus medius/maximus; excess hip adduction and medial rotation "pushes" the patella. (Lecture 10)

questions.q: Which ligament is typically injured first in a lateral ankle sprain?
questions.explanation: Inversion + plantarflexion → ATFL (± CFL). (Lecture 11)

questions.q: A high (syndesmotic) ankle sprain is caused by:
questions.explanation: Syndesmotic sprain = external rotation + dorsiflexion, injuring distal tibiofibular ligaments; squeeze test. (Lecture 11)

questions.q: The deltoid ligament prevents excessive:
questions.explanation: Medial (deltoid) complex prevents excessive eversion; very strong, rarely injured. (Lecture 11)

questions.q: Which is one of the Ottawa ankle rule criteria?
options: Bony tenderness at the base of the 5th metatarsal
questions.explanation: Ottawa: distal 6 cm posterior fibula/lateral malleolus, distal 6 cm posterior tibia/medial malleolus, base of 5th MT, navicular, inability to bear weight 4 steps. (Lecture 11)

questions.q: A positive Thompson test (no plantarflexion when the calf is squeezed) indicates:
questions.explanation: Thompson test for Achilles rupture – more common in men 30–40s. (Lecture 11)

questions.q: Morton's neuroma most commonly occurs in the:
questions.explanation: Compressive neuropathy of the common plantar digital nerve, most commonly 3rd web space; Mulder's click. (Lecture 11)

questions.q: Tarsal tunnel syndrome is entrapment of the:
questions.explanation: Also called posterior tibial nerve neuralgia; positive Tinel's sign. (Lecture 11)

questions.q: Plantar fasciitis typically causes:
options: Medial heel pain worst with the first steps in the morning
questions.explanation: Medial heel pain, worse on first steps; point tenderness at the medial calcaneal tubercle. (Lecture 11)

questions.q: The most common long bone fracture is the:
questions.explanation: Tibia shaft = most common long bone fracture; complications include compartment syndrome. (Lecture 11)

questions.q: Which compartment syndrome sign is a LATE finding?
questions.explanation: Peripheral pulses absent = late finding. (Lecture 11)

questions.q: Which zone of 5th metatarsal fracture is the Jones fracture?
questions.explanation: Zone 1 tuberosity avulsion (good blood supply); Zone 2 Jones; Zone 3 proximal diaphyseal stress fracture. (Lecture 11)

questions.q: Pilon (tibial plafond) fractures are usually treated by:
options: Staged surgery – temporary external fixation then delayed ORIF
questions.explanation: Stage 1 external fixation ("damage control"); stage 2 ORIF after 7–14 days. (Lecture 11)

questions.q: Clubfoot deformity is summarised by the acronym CAVE, which stands for:
questions.explanation: Cavus, adducted forefoot, varus hindfoot, equinus. (Lecture 12)

questions.q: The gold-standard treatment for clubfoot is:
questions.explanation: Ponseti = manipulation + serial casting + percutaneous tenotomy + abduction brace (~95% success). (Lecture 12)

questions.q: Osgood-Schlatter disease is:
options: Osteochondrosis of the tibial tubercle from repetitive knee extensor contraction
Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
A growth plate fracture of the distal radius
questions.explanation: Inflammation of the patellar ligament on the tibial tubercle; conservative care successful in 90%. (Lecture 12)

questions.q: In infants younger than 4 months, the imaging of choice for hip dysplasia is:
questions.explanation: US <4 months (hip mainly cartilaginous); radiograph after 4 months. (Lecture 12)

questions.q: The Ortolani manoeuvre:
options: Abducts the hip, relocating the femoral head into the acetabulum (click)
Adducts the hip with posterior pressure to dislocate it
questions.explanation: Barlow = adduction + posterior pressure; Ortolani = abduction, femoral head back in (click). (Lecture 12)

questions.q: Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease is:
options: Idiopathic juvenile avascular necrosis of the femoral head
questions.explanation: Juvenile AVN of the femoral head, peak 5–7 y, M:F 5:1; phases: necrosis, fragmentation, reossification, remodelling. (Lecture 12)

questions.q: In Perthes disease, prognosis is best when onset is:
questions.explanation: <6 y benign course; 6–8 variable; >8 poor with conservative treatment. (Lecture 12)

questions.q: The most common indication for lower limb amputation is:
questions.explanation: PVD ≈70% of lower limb cases; upper limb amputations mostly result from trauma. (Lecture 13)

questions.q: A transtibial amputation increases energy expenditure by about:
questions.explanation: Transtibial +25–40%; transfemoral +65–100%; Syme/Pirogoff +10–20%. (Lecture 13)

questions.q: Which contracture tends to develop in a short transfemoral stump?
questions.explanation: Weak adductors → flexion and abduction contracture; long stumps give the best lever. (Lecture 13)

questions.q: A Syme amputation is:
options: Ankle disarticulation with removal of the malleoli
Disarticulation through the talonavicular and calcaneocuboid joints
questions.explanation: Syme = ankle disarticulation; Lisfranc = tarsometatarsal; Chopart = talonavicular/calcaneocuboid. (Lecture 13)

questions.q: Phantom limb sensation occurs in up to:
questions.explanation: Incidence up to 80%; mechanisms include cortical reorganisation, neuroma, central sensitisation. Mirror therapy gives short-term relief. (Lecture 13)

questions.q: A myoelectric prosthesis is controlled by:
options: EMG signals detected from residual muscles
No active control – it is cosmetic
questions.explanation: Myoelectric = surface electrodes detect EMG; body-powered = cable/harness. (Lecture 13)

questions.q: Closed reduction is:
options: Moving the bone back into place without cutting the skin, then holding it with a cast or splint
Opening the skin and fixing the bone with plates and screws
Replacing the joint with a prosthesis
questions.explanation: Closed reduction = manual realignment through the skin + cast/splint. (Basics doc)

questions.q: ORIF is typically chosen for:
options: Severe, displaced or complex fractures that cannot be held by a cast
questions.explanation: ORIF = surgical open reduction + internal fixation for displaced/complex/unstable breaks. (Basics doc)

questions.q: Which is a main risk of ORIF (rather than closed reduction)?
options: Healing crooked because the cast slipped
questions.explanation: ORIF risks: infection, nerve irritation, hardware issues. Closed reduction risks: re-displacement, malunion, stiffness. (Basics doc)

questions.q: Arthroplasty differs from ORIF because it:
options: Replaces damaged joint components with prosthetic implants
questions.explanation: Arthroplasty removes damaged bone/cartilage and replaces it with implants; often allows early weight-bearing. (Basics doc)

classes.title: Biomechanics
classes.desc: Kinematics, kinetics, gait analysis, measurement, posture, knee, hip, spine

questions.q: Kinematics is the branch of mechanics that:
options: Describes how a body moves without considering the forces causing the motion
Studies the forces that cause or resist motion
questions.explanation: Kinetics explains why a body moves (forces); kinematics describes how. (Concepts I)

questions.q: A biomechanical model represents the body as:
options: Rigid bodies linked by joints, moving in 3D space under internal and external forces
A single point mass with no joints
questions.explanation: Concepts I, biomechanical model slide.

questions.q: In the course's orthogonal reference system, the z-axis represents:
questions.explanation: x = forward–backward, y = side-to-side, z = vertical. (Concepts I)

questions.q: Which is a SCALAR quantity?
questions.explanation: A scalar has only magnitude. Displacement, velocity and weight are vectors (magnitude, direction, point of application). (Concepts I)

questions.q: You fly Barcelona→Rome (850 km) and back. Your displacement is:
questions.explanation: Displacement is a vector: +850 + (−850) = 0; distance (scalar) is 1700 km. (Concepts I)

questions.q: A 70 kg person on the Moon (g = 1.62 m/s²) has:
options: The same mass (70 kg) but a weight of about 113 N
The same weight as on Earth (686 N)
questions.explanation: Mass does not change with location; W = m·g. (Concepts I)

questions.q: The SI unit of torque is:
questions.explanation: Pressure Pa (N/m²), work J, power W (J/s), torque N·m. (Concepts I)

questions.q: In quiet standing, the body's centre of mass lies approximately:
options: At pelvis level, in front of L4–L5
At the level of the sternum
Behind the sacrum outside the body
questions.explanation: Concepts I. (The posture lecture describes it as approximately at the 2nd sacral segment.)

questions.q: When the arms are raised overhead, the CoM:
questions.explanation: CoM depends on mass distribution and posture. (Concepts I)

questions.q: The Base of Support is:
options: The area within the perimeter of all contact points with the supporting surface
The point of application of the GRF
questions.explanation: The CoP can only move within the BoS. (Concepts I)

questions.q: Balance (vs stability) is defined as:
options: The ability to keep the CoM within the BoS, statically or while moving
The ability to return to the original position after a perturbation
questions.explanation: Stability = returning to original position after a perturbation without losing balance. (Concepts I)

questions.q: A cane or a wider stance improves balance mainly by:
questions.explanation: Concepts I – strategies to reduce fall risk.

questions.q: Flexion–extension occurs around which axis and in which plane?
questions.explanation: Ab/adduction: sagittal axis, frontal plane; rotations: vertical axis, transverse plane. (Concepts I)

questions.q: The sagittal plane divides the body into:
questions.explanation: Frontal = anterior/posterior; transverse = superior/inferior. (Concepts I)

questions.q: When measuring knee flexion with a goniometer, the fulcrum is placed on:
options: The lateral epicondyle of the femur
questions.explanation: Stationary arm with thigh (towards greater trochanter), moving arm with fibula/lateral malleolus. (Concepts I; Knee)

questions.q: How many degrees of freedom define a rigid segment's position in 3D space?
questions.explanation: Concepts I – DoF slide.

questions.q: According to the course DoF table, the wrist (radiocarpal + midcarpal) is modelled as:
options: A universal (ellipsoid) joint with 2 rotational DoF
questions.explanation: Elbow hinge 1, radio-ulnar pivot 1, hip/shoulder spherical 3, ankle hinge 1, subtalar pivot 1. (Concepts I)

questions.q: Optical motion capture reconstructs 3D marker position by stereo-triangulation, requiring:
options: At least two cameras to see each marker simultaneously
A force plate under the subject
questions.explanation: More cameras → more redundancy → higher accuracy. (Concepts I)

questions.q: Typical MoCap camera sampling rates quoted are:
questions.explanation: Concepts I – motion capture system.

questions.q: The gait cycle is defined as:
options: The events between two successive initial contacts of the same foot
One step from right to left foot
questions.explanation: Concepts I / Gait analysis.

questions.q: In normal adult walking (~1.2 m/s), the stance period is about:
questions.explanation: Stance ≈60%, swing ≈40%, each double support ≈10%. (Concepts I)

questions.q: Which phase starts at about 60% of the gait cycle?
Stride length equals:
options: Two step lengths – distance between successive contacts of the same foot
questions.explanation: Concepts I – spatial parameters.

questions.q: Walking speed equals:
questions.explanation: A child next to an adult must raise cadence due to shorter stride. (Concepts I)

questions.q: A normalised walking speed of 50–100% of height corresponds to:
questions.explanation: <30% weight transfers, 30–50% slow, 50–100% normal, >100% running. (Concepts I)

questions.q: Why is temporal normalisation (0–100%) used in movement analysis?
options: To reduce inter- and intra-subject variability so trials can be compared
questions.explanation: Concepts I.

questions.q: An increased hip flexion angle in gait could be due to:
options: Increased femoral flexion OR increased anterior pelvic tilt
questions.explanation: Joint angles are relative, not absolute. (Concepts I)

questions.q: During walking, pelvic "obliquity" describes rotation around which axis?
options: No axis – it is a translation
questions.explanation: Tilt around Y; obliquity around X; rotation around Z. (Concepts I)

questions.q: Moment of inertia (I = m·r²) means that:
options: Mass farther from the axis makes a segment harder to rotate
questions.explanation: Bending the knee during swing reduces I so the leg moves faster. (Concepts II)

questions.q: Newton's 2nd law for rotation states:
questions.explanation: Linear F = m·a; rotational torque = moment of inertia × angular acceleration. (Concepts II)

questions.q: A 10 N force on a 0.62 kg basketball produces about 16 m/s². A billiard ball of one quarter the mass would receive:
questions.explanation: a = F/m. (Concepts II)

questions.q: Torque is zero when:
options: The line of action of the force passes through the axis of rotation
questions.explanation: T = d × F; d = 0. (Concepts II)

questions.q: Holding a 50 N load, elbow torque at 90° is 15 N·m (d = 0.30 m). At 30° (d = 0.08 m) it is:
questions.explanation: Moment arm changes during movement. (Concepts II)

questions.q: Which is an EXTERNAL force?
questions.explanation: Internal: muscle, ligament, joint reaction. External: gravity, GRF, external load, wind, friction. (Concepts II)

questions.q: In a first-class lever:
options: The fulcrum lies between effort and resistance
The resistance lies between fulcrum and effort
The effort lies between fulcrum and resistance
questions.explanation: Course example: supraspinatus/upper limb. (Concepts II)

questions.q: The course example of a second-class lever (effort arm > resistance arm) is:
questions.explanation: Concepts II. (Wheelbarrow is the everyday example.)

questions.q: The biceps flexing the elbow is a:
questions.explanation: Effort between fulcrum and resistance; MA < 1 but more speed and ROM. (Concepts II)

questions.q: Mechanical advantage is the ratio:
options: Resistance / Effort (= effort arm / resistance arm)
questions.explanation: MA > 1 = advantage. (Concepts II)

questions.q: The patella improves knee extension by:
options: Increasing the quadriceps lever arm, reducing the mechanical disadvantage
Converting it to a first-class lever
questions.explanation: Example MA 0.1 → 0.3. (Concepts II; Knee lecture: patella increases quadriceps moment arm.)

questions.q: Leaning the trunk forward when climbing a step:
options: Reduces the resistance moment arm and the quadriceps force needed
questions.explanation: Example: required quadriceps force drops from >658 N to >278 N. (Concepts II)

questions.q: Momentum is:
questions.explanation: Angular momentum L = I·ω. (Concepts II)

questions.q: Impulse equals:
options: Force applied over time = change in momentum
questions.explanation: J = ∫F·dt = ΔP. (Concepts II)

questions.q: Mechanical work is:
questions.explanation: Work is positive if force and displacement in same direction. (Concepts II)

questions.q: Negative muscular work corresponds to:
options: Eccentric contraction – absorbing energy and decelerating the segment
questions.explanation: Concepts II.

questions.q: In an isometric contraction:
options: Work and power are zero even if force is high
questions.explanation: No displacement → no work or power. (Concepts II)

questions.q: Isokinetic testing at low speeds (e.g. 60°/s) mainly assesses:
questions.explanation: Higher velocities (e.g. 180°/s) assess power. (Concepts II)

questions.q: With ageing, muscle power is reported to decrease:
questions.explanation: Sit-to-stand example: 300 W young vs 60 W older. (Concepts II)

questions.q: In walking, potential and kinetic energy are:
options: Out of phase – an inverted-pendulum exchange
questions.explanation: In running they are in phase; efficiency relies on elastic energy storage. (Concepts II)

questions.q: The CoM is at its highest point, with maximal potential energy, during:
questions.explanation: In running, CoM is lowest in mid-stance. (Concepts II)

questions.q: In quiet standing, the GRF is:
options: Equal in magnitude and opposite to body weight, collinear with it
questions.explanation: Concepts II.

questions.q: If the CoM accelerates downward when landing, vertical GRF:
questions.explanation: GRF increases with negative (downward) acceleration and decreases with upward acceleration.

questions.q: The anterior–posterior GRF component represents:
questions.explanation: Vertical = support; ML = weight shifts. (Concepts II)

questions.q: For walking velocity to remain constant:
options: The braking impulse must equal the propulsive impulse
questions.explanation: Conservation of AP momentum. (Concepts II)

questions.q: At initial contact the ankle dorsiflexors work:
options: Eccentrically to prevent the foot from dropping (power absorption)
questions.explanation: Concepts II – ankle power.

questions.q: The main positive ankle power peak in gait comes from:
options: Rapid concentric plantar-flexor contraction at push-off
questions.explanation: Concepts II.

questions.q: If torque is normal but ankle power is reduced, a likely cause is:
questions.explanation: Power = torque × angular velocity. (Concepts II)

questions.q: A force platform records:
options: The three GRF components and the CoP coordinates
questions.explanation: Concepts II.

questions.q: Clinical gait analysis is defined as:
options: Recording and interpreting biomechanical measurements of walking to support clinical decisions
questions.explanation: Baker et al. It can help differential diagnosis but is not the definitive diagnostic tool. (Gait analysis)

questions.q: Compared with conventional physical examination, gait analysis is:
questions.explanation: Gait analysis lecture.

questions.q: Basic gait lab equipment includes:
options: 3D optoelectronic system, force platforms and surface EMG
questions.explanation: Gait analysis lecture.

questions.q: In the SIAMOC model, who performs the test and manages the patient?
questions.explanation: Physician: exam and clinical interpretation; bioengineer: biomechanical interpretation and equipment. (Gait analysis)

questions.q: Gait analysis is Class I, Level B evidence for influencing:
options: Functional surgery planning in infantile cerebral palsy
questions.explanation: Acquired brain injury Class I Level C; amputation Class II Level C. (Gait analysis)

questions.q: The Ely test assesses tightness of:
questions.explanation: Thomas = iliopsoas; popliteal angle = hamstrings; Ober = TFL/ITB. (Gait analysis; Knee)

questions.q: MMT grade 3 means:
options: Movement against gravity but not resistance
questions.explanation: Gait analysis lecture.

questions.q: A cavus foot is characterised by:
options: Increased arch, rigid foot and reduced pronation/shock absorption
questions.explanation: Gait analysis – footprint slide.

questions.q: The first vertical GRF peak in stance corresponds to:
options: The downward drop of the CoM after foot loading
questions.explanation: GRF peaks: 1 posterior (shock absorption), 2 first vertical (downward drop), 3 upward CoM, 4 zero AP, 5 second vertical, 6 anterior (push-off). (Gait analysis)

questions.q: During shock absorption, which muscles work eccentrically?
options: Gluteus medius/TFL, quadriceps and tibialis anterior
questions.explanation: Gait analysis GRF1.

questions.q: Iliopsoas tightness in gait mainly limits:
questions.explanation: Rectus femoris tightness limits knee flexion in swing. (Gait analysis)

questions.q: Spasticity is defined as:
options: A velocity-dependent increase in muscle resistance to passive stretch
questions.explanation: Clonus is rhythmic involuntary contraction at 5–7 Hz. (Gait analysis)

questions.q: The "double bump" in swing with gastrocnemius spasticity is:
options: A spastic plantarflexion reaction when attempting active dorsiflexion
questions.explanation: Gait analysis.

questions.q: The pendulum test assesses spasticity of:
questions.explanation: Free swinging of the relaxed lower limb. (Gait analysis)

questions.q: In the crouch-gait case, the main cause identified was:
questions.explanation: Main indication: hamstring and iliopsoas stretches; no BT-A in triceps surae because of weakness. (Gait analysis)

questions.q: Reliability is:
options: The degree to which a measure is consistent and free of error
Assigning clinical meaning to a score
questions.explanation: Validity = measuring what is intended; responsiveness = detecting change. (Reliability)

questions.q: Which statement is TRUE?
options: A measurement can be reliable without being valid, but not valid without being reliable
A valid test is never reliable
questions.explanation: Reliability lecture.

questions.q: Systematic error (e.g. calibration error) mainly affects:
questions.explanation: Random error is the main subject of reliability studies. (Reliability)

questions.q: A reliability coefficient above 0.75 is considered:
questions.explanation: <0.5 poor, 0.5–0.75 fair, >0.75 good; >0.9 recommended for diagnostic parameters. (Reliability)

questions.q: Correlation differs from agreement because correlation measures:
options: Association, while agreement measures identity between measurements
questions.explanation: Reliability lecture.

questions.q: Which coefficient is used for internal consistency of scales?
questions.explanation: Kappa for categorical test-retest; ICC for relative reliability. (Reliability)

questions.q: Bland–Altman limits of agreement are calculated as:
options: Mean difference ± 2 SD of the differences
